subject: Biology
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 2-hour practical test worth 80 marks: Nigerian candidates answer two compulsory Section A questions (25 marks each) and one Section C question (30 marks). Questions are set on specimens, experiments and results provided, testing identification, observation, drawing with labels and magnification, simple tests and calculations from experimental data.

practicals.title: Using the light microscope: onion epidermal cells
practicals.aim: To prepare a temporary mount of onion epidermis, observe plant cells under the light microscope and calculate magnification and actual cell size.
safety: Carry the microscope with one hand under the base and the other on the arm.
Cut away from your fingers when using the scalpel or razor blade.
Never focus downwards with the coarse adjustment while looking through the eyepiece, or the objective may crack the slide.
procedure: Cut an onion bulb into quarters and remove one fleshy scale leaf.
Snap the scale leaf and use forceps to peel off the thin, transparent epidermis from its inner (concave) surface.
Place a drop of water on a clean slide and lay a small square (about 5 mm) of the epidermis flat in it, avoiding folds.
Add one drop of dilute iodine solution to stain the nuclei and starch.
Lower a cover slip at an angle of about 45° using a mounted needle so that air bubbles are not trapped; blot off excess liquid.
Place the slide on the stage, start with the low-power (×10) objective and focus with the coarse adjustment, raising the tube away from the slide.
Centre a group of cells, switch to the high-power (×40) objective and focus with the fine adjustment only.
Draw three or four adjacent cells, label the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuole, and state the magnification of the drawing.
practicals.expectedObservations: Brick-shaped, closely packed cells arranged in rows with no air spaces. Each cell has a distinct cell wall, a thin layer of cytoplasm stained light yellow-brown, a large central vacuole and a darker brown, rounded nucleus usually pressed to one side. No chloroplasts are seen because the scale leaf grows underground and is not exposed to light.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. With a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective, magnification = 10 × 40 = ×400.
Actual size: the field of view under ×100 is 1.6 mm (1600 µm) wide. Under ×400 the field is 1600 ÷ 4 = 400 µm wide. If 4 cells lie end to end across the field, one cell is about 400 ÷ 4 = 100 µm long (0.1 mm).
Drawing magnification = length of drawing ÷ actual length. A cell drawn 50 mm (50 000 µm) long that is actually 100 µm long is drawn at 50 000 ÷ 100 = ×500.
precautions: Use a thin, single layer of epidermis so that light passes through.
Lower the cover slip gently to avoid air bubbles.
Clean lenses only with lens tissue.
Always start focusing with the low-power objective.
sourcesOfError: Air bubbles mistaken for cells (they have thick black outlines).
Folded epidermis giving overlapping cells.
Estimating cell numbers across the field of view by eye.
commonMistakes: Drawing cells as circles instead of brick shapes.
Labelling chloroplasts in onion cells.
Shading drawings instead of using clean single lines.
Forgetting to state the magnification of the drawing.
examTips: Marks are given for size (at least half the space provided), clarity of lines, correct labels with ruled guide lines that do not cross, and a title with magnification.
State why iodine is used (to stain the nucleus so it is visible).
Explain the absence of chloroplasts — a frequent short question.

checkQuestions.q: A student uses a ×15 eyepiece and a ×40 objective. What is the total magnification?
checkQuestions.explanation: Total magnification is the product: 15 × 40 = ×600.

checkQuestions.q: Why are chloroplasts absent from onion scale-leaf epidermal cells?
options: The scale leaves are underground and receive no light
Onion is not a flowering plant
They are too small to be seen at ×400
checkQuestions.explanation: Onion scale leaves are storage leaves in a bulb, kept from light, so they do not develop chloroplasts.

checkQuestions.q: What is the main purpose of lowering the cover slip at an angle?
options: To prevent trapping of air bubbles
checkQuestions.explanation: Lowering at an angle pushes air out ahead of the slip.

practicals.title: Animal cells: human cheek epithelium
practicals.aim: To prepare and observe a temporary mount of human cheek cells and compare animal cells with plant cells.
apparatus: Sterile cotton bud or clean wooden spatula
safety: Each student must use only their own cheek cells and a fresh cotton bud.
Put used buds, slides and cover slips straight into disinfectant.
Methylene blue stains skin and clothes; handle with care.
procedure: Rinse your mouth with clean water.
Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a fresh cotton bud.
Smear the bud on the centre of a clean slide containing a drop of water.
Add one drop of dilute methylene blue and leave for one minute.
Lower a cover slip carefully and blot excess stain.
Examine under low power, then high power, and draw two or three cells with labels.
Place the bud and slide in disinfectant immediately after use.
practicals.expectedObservations: Flat, irregular, roughly polygonal cells, often scattered singly or in small sheets. Each cell has a thin cell (plasma) membrane, granular cytoplasm stained pale blue and a darker blue, central nucleus. There is no cell wall, no large central vacuole and no chloroplast.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Cell size by field of view: at ×400 the field diameter is 0.40 mm (400 µm). If about 6.5 cells fit across, each cell is roughly 400 ÷ 6.5 ≈ 62 µm wide.
Comparison of size: an onion cell of 100 µm is about 100 ÷ 62 ≈ 1.6 times as long as the cheek cell.
precautions: Scrape gently; you need loose surface cells only.
Use only a little stain so cells are not over-darkened.
Do not share cotton buds.
sourcesOfError: Cells clumped and folded so outlines are unclear.
Food particles or bacteria mistaken for cells.
commonMistakes: Drawing a cell wall or vacuole in an animal cell.
Drawing cells touching in neat rows like plant cells.
Using the wrong stain name in the answer.
examTips: Tabulate differences between plant and animal cells (wall, vacuole, chloroplast, shape); each correct pair earns a mark.
The word 'cell membrane' is expected, not 'cell wall', for animal cells.

checkQuestions.q: Which structure would you NOT see in a cheek cell?
checkQuestions.explanation: Animal cells lack a cellulose cell wall.

checkQuestions.q: Methylene blue is used in this practical to
options: fix the cells to the slide
checkQuestions.explanation: It stains the nucleus darker blue so it can be seen.

checkQuestions.q: Used cotton buds should be
checkQuestions.explanation: They carry saliva and possible pathogens, so they are disinfected.

practicals.title: Pond water: unicellular and colonial organisms
practicals.topic: Forms in which Living Cells Exist
practicals.aim: To observe living organisms in pond water and identify single-celled, colonial and filamentous forms such as Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, Euglena, Volvox and Spirogyra.
materials: Pond or stagnant water sample with green scum
Cotton wool fibres (to slow fast swimmers)
safety: Wash hands with soap after handling pond water.
Do not drink or splash pond water; it may carry pathogens.
procedure: Collect water and some green scum from a pond or roadside pool in a clean bottle.
Place a drop from near the bottom or the green scum on a cavity slide with a few cotton fibres.
Cover with a cover slip and examine under low power.
Move the slide slowly to search; switch to high power when an organism is found.
Record the shape, colour, movement and any visible organelles (flagella, cilia, chloroplasts, contractile vacuole).
Draw and label one single-celled organism, one colony and one filament.
practicals.expectedObservations: Chlamydomonas: small green oval cell with two flagella and a cup-shaped chloroplast, moving rapidly. Euglena: spindle-shaped green cell with one flagellum and a red eyespot. Paramecium: slipper-shaped, covered with cilia, colourless. Amoeba: irregular, changing shape with pseudopodia. Volvox: hollow green sphere made of many cells. Spirogyra: unbranched green filament with spiral chloroplasts.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Speed of a swimming organism: a Paramecium crosses a 400 µm field of view in 2 s. Speed = distance ÷ time = 400 ÷ 2 = 200 µm/s (0.2 mm/s).
In 1 minute it would travel 200 × 60 = 12 000 µm = 12 mm.
precautions: Use cotton fibres to slow fast swimmers.
Do not let the slide dry out under the lamp; add water if needed.
Search systematically across the slide.
sourcesOfError: Organisms swim out of view before they can be drawn.
Debris mistaken for organisms.
commonMistakes: Calling Volvox a single cell rather than a colony.
Confusing cilia (many, short) with flagella (few, long).
Drawing Spirogyra with ring-shaped instead of spiral chloroplasts.
examTips: WAEC often gives drawings or descriptions and asks for the name, kingdom and one feature for identification.
State one adaptive feature linked to function, e.g. the eyespot of Euglena detects light for photosynthesis.

checkQuestions.q: Which organism moves by pseudopodia?
checkQuestions.explanation: Amoeba flows its cytoplasm into pseudopodia.

checkQuestions.q: Volvox is best described as a
checkQuestions.explanation: Volvox is a colony of many similar cells in a hollow sphere.

checkQuestions.q: Spirogyra can be identified by its
checkQuestions.explanation: Each cell contains one or more spiral, ribbon-shaped chloroplasts.

practicals.title: Osmosis in potato cylinders
practicals.aim: To investigate the effect of sucrose (or salt) solution concentration on the length and mass of Irish potato cylinders and estimate the concentration of the cell sap.
safety: Push the cork borer into the tuber on a tile, away from the hand.
Cut on a white tile, never on your palm.
procedure: Use the cork borer to cut five cylinders from the same tuber and remove any skin.
Trim each cylinder to exactly 50.0 mm with a scalpel on a tile.
Blot each cylinder dry, weigh it and record initial length and mass.
Place one cylinder in each labelled beaker containing the same volume of solution so that it is fully covered.
Leave for at least 1 hour (better 2 hours) at room temperature.
Remove each cylinder with forceps, blot gently and record final length and mass, and note whether it is firm or flaccid.
Calculate the percentage change for each and plot percentage change against concentration.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cylinders in distilled water and weak solutions become longer, heavier and firm (turgid). Those in strong solutions become shorter, lighter and soft/flaccid. At one concentration there is almost no change.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
% change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100.
Results (initial 50.0 mm): 0.0 → 54.0 mm (+8.0%); 0.2 → 52.0 mm (+4.0%); 0.4 → 49.5 mm (−1.0%); 0.6 → 47.5 mm (−5.0%); 0.8 → 46.0 mm (−8.0%).
The graph crosses 0% between 0.2 and 0.4 mol/dm³. By linear interpolation: 0.2 + (4.0 ÷ (4.0 + 1.0)) × 0.2 = 0.2 + 0.16 = 0.36 mol/dm³. This is the estimated concentration of the potato cell sap (the solution isotonic with the cells).
precautions: Cut all cylinders from the same tuber with the same borer.
Blot each cylinder in the same way before measuring.
Fully immerse cylinders and use equal volumes of solution.
Keep the time the same for all cylinders.
sourcesOfError: Unequal blotting leaves different amounts of surface water.
Reading length to the nearest mm only.
Temperature changes during the experiment.
commonMistakes: Omitting the negative sign for decreases.
Using final length as the denominator.
Saying 'water moves from low to high concentration of water' — it moves from a region of higher water potential (dilute) to lower (concentrated).
examTips: Graph marks: title, labelled axes with units, suitable scale, accurate points, smooth line or straight line through points, and the 0% line drawn to read the isotonic point.
Explain changes using turgor, plasmolysis and the selectively permeable membrane.

checkQuestions.q: A 40 mm cylinder becomes 42 mm. Its percentage change is
A cylinder in 0.8 mol/dm³ sucrose became soft because it
checkQuestions.explanation: The solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they become flaccid.

checkQuestions.q: The point where the graph crosses 0% change shows the
options: isotonic concentration of the cell sap
checkQuestions.explanation: No net water movement occurs when the solution and cell sap are isotonic.

checkQuestions.q: Why are all cylinders cut from the same tuber?
options: Because other tubers have no cells
So that the cell sap concentration is the same
checkQuestions.explanation: Using one tuber keeps the starting cell sap concentration a controlled variable.

practicals.title: Plasmolysis in epidermal cells
practicals.aim: To observe plasmolysis and deplasmolysis in coloured epidermal cells placed in strong salt or sugar solution and in water.
materials: Red onion bulb, Rhoeo/Tradescantia leaf or red cabbage epidermis
safety: Handle slides and blades carefully.
Wash hands after the practical.
procedure: Peel a small piece of coloured epidermis and mount it in a drop of distilled water.
Observe under low then high power and draw two turgid cells.
Place a drop of strong salt solution at one edge of the cover slip and draw it under with filter paper at the opposite edge.
Wait 5–10 minutes and observe; count the cells showing plasmolysis in the field.
Replace the salt solution with distilled water in the same way and observe again after 10 minutes.
Draw labelled diagrams of a turgid and a plasmolysed cell.
practicals.expectedObservations: In water the coloured cytoplasm and vacuole fill the cell. In strong salt solution the vacuole shrinks, the coloured sap becomes darker and the cytoplasm pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis); the space between wall and membrane fills with outside solution. In water again the cells regain turgor (deplasmolysis).
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Percentage of plasmolysed cells: 36 out of 48 cells in the field show plasmolysis after 10 minutes. % plasmolysed = 36 ÷ 48 × 100 = 75%.
The solution at which 50% of cells are plasmolysed (incipient plasmolysis) is taken as roughly isotonic with the cell sap.
precautions: Draw the solution right under the cover slip.
Allow enough time before observing.
Use thin, single-layer epidermis.
sourcesOfError: Some cells damaged by peeling do not respond.
Evaporation under the lamp concentrating the solution.
commonMistakes: Drawing the cell wall shrinking — the wall is rigid and stays the same.
Saying salt enters the cell and causes shrinking.
examTips: Labels expected: cell wall, cell membrane, shrunken vacuole, cytoplasm, space filled with external solution.
Explain why plant cells do not burst in water (the cell wall resists expansion).

checkQuestions.q: During plasmolysis the part that does NOT shrink is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The cellulose cell wall is rigid and keeps its shape.

checkQuestions.q: The space between the wall and shrunken cytoplasm of a plasmolysed cell contains
checkQuestions.explanation: The cell wall is fully permeable, so the external solution fills the gap.

practicals.title: Diffusion and surface area to volume ratio
practicals.aim: To show diffusion using agar blocks containing an indicator and to relate the rate of diffusion to the surface area : volume ratio of the blocks.
materials: Agar jelly made with phenolphthalein and a little dilute sodium hydroxide (pink)
safety: Wear eye protection when handling acid and alkali.
Cut on a tile away from your hand.
Rinse spills with plenty of water.
procedure: Cut three cubes of pink agar with sides 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm.
Calculate surface area, volume and surface area : volume ratio for each cube.
Place all cubes at the same time into a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid so that they are fully covered.
Start the stopwatch and record the time taken for each cube to become completely colourless.
Alternatively, remove the cubes after 5 minutes, cut them in half and measure the depth of the colourless zone.
practicals.expectedObservations: The acid diffuses inwards and the pink colour disappears from the outside towards the centre. The smallest cube becomes colourless first; the largest takes the longest and may still have a pink centre after the same time.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
1 cm cube: area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, ratio 6 : 1. 2 cm cube: area 24 cm², volume 8 cm³, ratio 3 : 1. 3 cm cube: area 54 cm², volume 27 cm³, ratio 2 : 1.
If 3 mm of a cube decolourises in 5 minutes, the rate of diffusion = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 mm per minute. A 1 cm cube (5 mm to the centre) is fully colourless after about 5 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 8.3 minutes; a 3 cm cube (15 mm to the centre) needs about 15 ÷ 0.6 = 25 minutes.
precautions: Cut cubes accurately to size.
Put all cubes in the acid at the same time.
Use the same acid concentration and temperature throughout.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate cutting of the cubes.
Judging the exact moment the colour disappears.
commonMistakes: Saying the larger cube has the larger ratio.
Forgetting units (cm², cm³).
Confusing diffusion with osmosis — no membrane is involved here.
examTips: Link the result to why large organisms need transport and gas-exchange systems.
Show working for ratio calculations; each correct ratio earns a mark.

checkQuestions.q: The surface area : volume ratio of a 2 cm cube is
checkQuestions.explanation: Area 24 cm² ÷ volume 8 cm³ = 3 : 1.

checkQuestions.q: Which cube becomes colourless first?
options: The one with the largest volume
The one with the smallest ratio
The one with the largest ratio
checkQuestions.explanation: The smallest cube has the largest ratio and the shortest distance to the centre.

checkQuestions.q: Diffusion is the movement of particles from
options: low to high concentration using energy
dilute to concentrated solution through a membrane only
checkQuestions.explanation: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient; it needs no energy.

practicals.title: Identifying specimens from the kingdoms
practicals.aim: To examine common specimens and place them in their kingdoms, divisions or phyla using observable features.
materials: Preserved specimens or good photographs where live ones are not available
safety: Wash hands after handling specimens, especially fungi and soil animals.
Do not sniff or taste mould cultures.
procedure: Lay out the specimens labelled with letters only.
Examine each with a hand lens, noting colour, body form, presence of chlorophyll, segmentation, limbs, spores or seeds.
Record features in a table.
Use the features to assign each specimen to a kingdom and then to a phylum, division or class.
Draw one plant and one animal specimen and label at least five parts.
practicals.expectedObservations: Mushroom and Rhizopus: no chlorophyll, made of hyphae, reproduce by spores — Fungi. Moss: small, leafy, no true roots (rhizoids) — Bryophyta. Fern: fronds with sori on underside — Filicinophyta. Pine: needle leaves, cones — Coniferophyta. Maize and hibiscus: flowers and seeds — Angiospermophyta. Earthworm: segmented, no legs — Annelida. Snail: soft body, shell — Mollusca. Cockroach: jointed legs, exoskeleton — Arthropoda (Insecta). Tilapia, toad, lizard — Chordata (Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia).
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Sorting the 13 specimens listed: 2 fungi (mushroom, Rhizopus), 5 green plants (moss, fern, pine, maize, hibiscus) and 6 animals. Percentage of the specimens that are autotrophic (green plants) = 5 ÷ 13 × 100 ≈ 38.5%; percentage that are animals = 6 ÷ 13 × 100 ≈ 46.2%.
Dichotomous keys: with n specimens a key needs n − 1 pairs of contrasting statements, so 8 specimens need 7 couplets.
precautions: Handle specimens gently to avoid damaging diagnostic parts.
Use the same order of features for every specimen in the table.
sourcesOfError: Dried or damaged specimens lose features such as sori or hyphae.
Photographs may hide size and texture.
commonMistakes: Placing mushrooms in the plant kingdom.
Calling a spider an insect (it has eight legs and two body parts).
Calling ferns flowering plants.
examTips: When asked for 'observable features', give features you can see on the specimen, not textbook facts such as 'reproduces by alternation of generations'.
Correct spelling of phylum names matters; Arthropoda, not Arthopoda.

checkQuestions.q: A green plant with fronds bearing brown sori on the underside belongs to
checkQuestions.explanation: Sori containing sporangia on fronds are typical of ferns.

checkQuestions.q: Rhizopus is placed in kingdom Fungi because it
options: is made of hyphae and lacks chlorophyll
checkQuestions.explanation: Fungi are non-green and made of hyphae.

checkQuestions.q: How many couplets does a dichotomous key need for 6 specimens?
checkQuestions.explanation: A dichotomous key for n specimens needs n − 1 couplets.

checkQuestions.q: Which specimen is an arthropod?
checkQuestions.explanation: Cockroaches have jointed legs and an exoskeleton.

practicals.title: Mammalian vertebrae
practicals.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
practicals.aim: To identify and draw the different types of mammalian vertebrae and relate their features to their functions.
materials: Cleaned vertebrae of goat, sheep or cow: atlas, axis, cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and caudal
safety: Bones should be boiled, cleaned and dried before use.
Wash hands after handling specimens.
procedure: Examine each vertebra in anterior view and side view.
Note the size and shape of the centrum, neural spine, transverse processes, neural canal and any facets or foramina.
Identify each vertebra using its distinctive features.
Draw the atlas and a lumbar vertebra in anterior view, about 8–10 cm high, and label.
Measure and record the height of the neural spine of the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae.
practicals.expectedObservations: Atlas: ring-shaped, no centrum, broad flat transverse processes, large facets for the occipital condyles. Axis: odontoid process (peg) projecting forward. Cervical: small neural spine, vertebrarterial canals in transverse processes. Thoracic: long backward-pointing neural spine, facets for ribs. Lumbar: large centrum, long broad transverse processes pointing forward, extra processes for muscle attachment. Sacral: fused into the sacrum. Caudal: small, reduced to a centrum in the tail.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Drawing magnification: an atlas 6.0 cm wide is drawn 12.0 cm wide. Magnification = 12.0 ÷ 6.0 = ×2.
Spine height: thoracic neural spine 7.2 cm, lumbar 3.6 cm. The thoracic spine is 7.2 ÷ 3.6 = 2 times as long, giving a large area for attaching neck and back muscles that support the head.
precautions: Draw in the correct view stated in the question.
Do not shade; use clear single lines.
sourcesOfError: Broken processes on old specimens.
Confusing lumbar and thoracic vertebrae in small animals.
commonMistakes: Labelling the odontoid process on the atlas.
Drawing vertebrae in side view when anterior view is asked.
Forgetting to give the magnification.
examTips: State features that adapt each vertebra to its function, e.g. the atlas facets allow nodding.
The axis–atlas joint (pivot) allows rotation of the head — a frequent question.

checkQuestions.q: Which vertebra has an odontoid process?
checkQuestions.explanation: The odontoid process of the axis fits into the atlas and acts as a pivot.

checkQuestions.q: Vertebrarterial canals are found in
checkQuestions.explanation: They carry the vertebral arteries in the neck.

checkQuestions.q: A thoracic vertebra is identified by
checkQuestions.explanation: Thoracic vertebrae carry the ribs.

practicals.title: Limb bones, girdles and joints
practicals.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
practicals.aim: To identify the bones of the limbs and girdles of a mammal and the types of joints they form.
materials: Cleaned bones: scapula, humerus, radius and ulna, pelvic girdle, femur, tibia and fibula
safety: Use cleaned and dried bones only.
Wash hands after handling.
procedure: Identify each bone by its shape and processes.
Fit the head of the humerus into the glenoid cavity and the head of the femur into the acetabulum to show the ball-and-socket joints.
Fit the humerus to the radius and ulna to show the hinge joint at the elbow.
Move the joints and record the directions of movement possible.
Draw the femur and the scapula and label their parts.
practicals.expectedObservations: Scapula: flat triangular bone with a spine and a glenoid cavity. Humerus: rounded head, deltoid ridge, trochlea at the lower end. Ulna: olecranon process (elbow) and sigmoid notch. Pelvic girdle: ilium, ischium, pubis fused around the acetabulum and obturator foramen. Femur: rounded head, neck, greater trochanter and condyles. Ball-and-socket joints allow movement in many planes; hinge joints allow movement in one plane only.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Range of movement at a hinge joint: if the forearm of a model moves from 30° to 160° measured with a protractor, range = 160 − 30 = 130° in one plane.
Length ratio: femur 22 cm, humerus 18 cm; femur : humerus = 22 ÷ 18 ≈ 1.2, showing hind limbs are longer for propulsion.
precautions: Hold bones in their correct orientation.
Do not force joints apart.
sourcesOfError: Damaged articular surfaces make fitting difficult.
Charts may not show processes clearly.
commonMistakes: Calling the elbow a ball-and-socket joint.
Mixing up radius and ulna (the ulna has the olecranon).
Confusing the acetabulum with the glenoid cavity.
examTips: Name the bone, the joint type and the movement it allows in a table.
Know which bones articulate at each joint; this is regularly tested.

checkQuestions.q: The head of the femur fits into the
checkQuestions.explanation: The acetabulum of the pelvic girdle receives the femur, forming a ball-and-socket joint.

checkQuestions.q: Which joint allows movement in one plane only?
checkQuestions.explanation: The knee is a hinge joint.

checkQuestions.q: The olecranon process is part of the
checkQuestions.explanation: The olecranon of the ulna forms the point of the elbow.

practicals.title: Transverse sections of dicot and monocot stems
practicals.aim: To cut and examine transverse sections of young dicot and monocot stems and identify supporting and conducting tissues.
materials: Young sunflower, Amaranthus or balsam stem (dicot)
safety: Cut away from fingers using a wet blade; hold the stem firmly.
Dispose of blades in a safe container.
procedure: Hold a short piece of stem upright and cut several very thin transverse sections with a wet razor blade.
Transfer sections with a brush into a watch glass of water.
Select the thinnest, most complete section and stain it for 2 minutes with safranin.
Mount in water under a cover slip and examine under low power.
Draw a low-power plan (tissue map) of each stem showing the distribution of tissues, without drawing individual cells.
Under high power identify collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem vessels and phloem.
practicals.expectedObservations: Dicot stem: vascular bundles arranged in a ring, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem outside, separated by cambium; collenchyma beneath the epidermis; large central pith. Monocot stem: many scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchyma sheath, no cambium, no distinct pith. Lignified xylem and sclerenchyma stain red with safranin.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Counting bundles: a sunflower section shows 16 bundles in a ring; a maize section shows about 120 scattered bundles in a sample area. Diameter of a xylem vessel: under ×400 the field is 400 µm wide and one vessel occupies about 1/10 of it, so vessel diameter ≈ 400 ÷ 10 = 40 µm.
precautions: Keep the blade and stem wet while cutting.
Choose the thinnest section, even if it is not a complete circle.
Draw a tissue plan only, with no cells, for low power.
sourcesOfError: Thick sections give overlapping cells.
Oblique cuts distort the shapes of vessels.
commonMistakes: Drawing individual cells in a low-power plan.
Placing phloem inside the xylem in dicot bundles.
Confusing pith with cortex.
examTips: Give at least three differences between monocot and dicot stems in a table.
Name the supporting tissues: collenchyma, sclerenchyma and lignified xylem.

checkQuestions.q: In a dicot stem the vascular bundles are
checkQuestions.explanation: Dicot stems have bundles in a ring around the pith.

checkQuestions.q: Which tissue stains red with safranin because it is lignified?
checkQuestions.explanation: Safranin stains lignin in xylem and sclerenchyma.

checkQuestions.q: A low-power plan of a stem should show
checkQuestions.explanation: Low-power plans outline tissue areas without cells.

checkQuestions.q: Cambium is absent from the vascular bundles of
checkQuestions.explanation: Monocots such as maize lack cambium in their bundles.

practicals.title: Measuring the rate of transpiration with a potometer
practicals.aim: To measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot using a bubble potometer and investigate the effect of environmental conditions such as wind and light.
apparatus: Bubble potometer with capillary tube and scale (mm)
materials: Freshly cut leafy shoot (e.g. hibiscus, Ixora or Acalypha)
safety: Keep the fan and electrical leads away from water.
Handle the glass capillary tube with care.
procedure: Cut the shoot under water at a slant so that air does not enter the xylem.
Fit the shoot into the potometer under water and seal the joint with Vaseline so it is airtight.
Remove the apparatus from the water, dry the leaves and allow one air bubble into the capillary tube.
When the bubble moves steadily, record its position and start the stopwatch.
Record the distance moved in 5 minutes in still air; reset the bubble with the reservoir tap.
Repeat with the fan blowing on the shoot, and in a dark cupboard, taking three readings each.
Calculate the mean distance per minute and the volume of water taken up for each condition.
practicals.expectedObservations: The bubble moves towards the shoot as water is taken up. It moves fastest in moving air (fan) and in bright light, and slowest in the dark or in still, humid air.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Capillary radius r = 0.5 mm. Cross-sectional area = πr² = 3.142 × 0.5² = 0.785 mm².
Still air: bubble moves 24 mm in 5 min → 4.8 mm/min → volume = 4.8 × 0.785 ≈ 3.77 mm³/min.
With fan: 60 mm in 5 min → 12 mm/min → 12 × 0.785 ≈ 9.42 mm³/min.
The fan increased the rate by (12 − 4.8) ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 150%.
precautions: Cut and fit the shoot under water.
Make all joints airtight with Vaseline.
Allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes before taking readings.
Keep the bubble in the scaled part of the tube.
sourcesOfError: Leaks at the joints.
Water uptake is not exactly equal to water lost (some is used in photosynthesis and to maintain turgor).
Changes in room temperature during the experiment.
commonMistakes: Saying the potometer measures transpiration directly — it measures water uptake.
Not converting distance to volume when asked.
Comparing only single readings instead of means.
examTips: State the assumption that the rate of uptake equals the rate of transpiration.
Explain wind removing water vapour and increasing the diffusion gradient; light opening the stomata.

checkQuestions.q: Why is the shoot cut under water?
options: To prevent air entering the xylem
checkQuestions.explanation: An air lock in the xylem would block water uptake.

checkQuestions.q: A bubble moves 30 mm in 6 min. The rate is
checkQuestions.explanation: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 mm per minute.

checkQuestions.q: A potometer actually measures
checkQuestions.explanation: It measures uptake, assumed to equal water loss.

checkQuestions.q: Which condition would give the slowest bubble movement?
checkQuestions.explanation: Closed stomata and a low diffusion gradient reduce transpiration.

practicals.title: Distribution of stomata on leaf surfaces
practicals.aim: To compare the numbers of stomata on the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf using cobalt chloride paper and nail-varnish impressions.
materials: Leaves of a dicot (e.g. hibiscus, cassava) and a monocot (e.g. maize)
safety: Use nail varnish in a ventilated room away from flames.
Do not touch cobalt chloride paper with wet hands; wash hands afterwards.
procedure: Fix a square of dry blue cobalt chloride paper on each surface of a leaf still attached to the plant using clear tape.
Record the time each paper takes to turn pink.
Paint a thin layer of clear nail varnish on a 1 cm² area of each surface of another leaf and allow it to dry.
Peel off the varnish with clear tape and stick it on a slide.
Count the stomata in the field of view at ×400 in five different fields for each surface.
Calculate the mean number per field and convert to stomata per mm².
practicals.expectedObservations: The cobalt chloride paper on the lower surface of the dicot leaf turns pink much faster than the paper on the upper surface. The impressions show many more stomata on the lower surface. In maize, both surfaces have similar numbers.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Field diameter at ×400 = 0.40 mm, so radius = 0.20 mm. Field area = πr² = 3.142 × 0.20² = 0.126 mm².
Mean count on lower surface = (28 + 31 + 25 + 30 + 26) ÷ 5 = 140 ÷ 5 = 28 per field. Stomatal density = 28 ÷ 0.126 ≈ 222 per mm².
Upper surface mean = 6 per field → 6 ÷ 0.126 ≈ 48 per mm². Ratio lower : upper ≈ 222 : 48 ≈ 4.6 : 1.
precautions: Use dry cobalt chloride paper.
Fix papers at the same time and on leaves of similar age.
Count stomata in several fields and find the mean.
sourcesOfError: Counting partly visible stomata at the edge of the field inconsistently.
Cobalt chloride paper absorbing moisture from the air.
commonMistakes: Concluding that stomata are absent from the upper surface.
Using the diameter instead of the radius in πr².
Forgetting the units per mm².
examTips: Explain the adaptation: fewer stomata on the upper surface reduces water loss in direct sunlight.
State the colour change correctly: blue to pink.

checkQuestions.q: Dry cobalt chloride paper turns from
checkQuestions.explanation: Anhydrous cobalt chloride is blue; with water it becomes pink.

checkQuestions.q: Why do most dicot leaves have more stomata on the lower surface?
options: Because the lower surface is thicker
checkQuestions.explanation: The lower surface is shaded and cooler, reducing water loss.

checkQuestions.q: If the mean is 10 stomata in a field of area 0.125 mm², the density is

practicals.title: Path of water in a plant using a dye
practicals.topic: Uptake and movement of water and mineral salts in plants
practicals.aim: To trace the path of water through the stem of a herbaceous plant using eosin (or red ink) and to locate the xylem.
materials: Young balsam (Impatiens) plant with roots, washed free of soil
safety: Eosin stains skin and clothes; avoid spills.
Cut away from your fingers.
procedure: Wash the roots of a balsam seedling carefully and stand them in a beaker of eosin solution.
Leave in a well-lit, airy place for 2–3 hours.
Note the stem and leaf veins as the red colour rises; record the height reached at intervals.
Cut transverse sections of the stem at different heights and examine with a hand lens or microscope.
Draw a section and shade the stained tissue.
practicals.expectedObservations: Red lines appear up the translucent stem and later in the leaf veins. Sections show the red dye only in the xylem of the vascular bundles arranged in a ring; the pith and cortex remain unstained.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: The dye reached 6.0 cm after 30 minutes and 15.0 cm after 90 minutes. Mean rate between 30 and 90 minutes = (15.0 − 6.0) ÷ (90 − 30) = 9.0 ÷ 60 = 0.15 cm/min (9 cm per hour).
precautions: Wash roots gently to avoid damaging root hairs.
Use a translucent-stemmed plant so the dye can be seen.
Cut thin sections.
sourcesOfError: Damaged roots let dye enter directly.
Dye spreading sideways in older stems.
commonMistakes: Saying the dye travels in the phloem.
Shading the whole stem section red in diagrams.
examTips: State clearly: the stained tissue is xylem, which conducts water and mineral salts.
Relate to forces: root pressure, capillarity and transpiration pull.

checkQuestions.q: In a stained stem section the red dye is found in the
checkQuestions.explanation: Water and dissolved substances move up in the xylem.

checkQuestions.q: Dye rises 12 cm in 40 minutes. The rate is
checkQuestions.explanation: 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 cm per minute.

checkQuestions.q: Placing the plant in a windy, bright place would make the dye rise
checkQuestions.explanation: Faster transpiration increases the transpiration pull.

practicals.title: External and internal structure of a mammalian heart
practicals.aim: To examine a fresh goat or cow heart and identify its chambers, valves and major blood vessels.
materials: Fresh goat, sheep or pig heart from the abattoir with vessels attached
safety: Wear gloves and wash hands after handling raw meat.
Cut away from yourself on a firm board.
Disinfect tools and surfaces afterwards.
procedure: Rinse the heart in water and identify the front (ventral) side by the diagonal coronary vessels.
Identify the atria, ventricles, aorta, pulmonary artery, venae cavae and pulmonary veins.
Push a glass rod into each vessel to find which chamber it enters.
Cut through the wall of the left and right ventricles from base to apex.
Compare the thickness of the ventricle walls and examine the valves and tendons (chordae tendineae).
Draw the internal structure and label the chambers, valves and vessels.
practicals.expectedObservations: The left ventricle wall is much thicker than the right. The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and ventricle; the bicuspid (mitral) valve between the left atrium and ventricle. Valve flaps are held by tendons attached to papillary muscles. Semilunar valves are found at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery. The aorta has a thick, elastic wall.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Wall thickness: left ventricle 15 mm, right ventricle 5 mm. Ratio = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 : 1, because the left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 cm³ × 72 beats/min = 5040 cm³/min ≈ 5.0 dm³/min.
precautions: Keep the vessels attached when buying the heart.
Cut carefully so that valves are not destroyed.
Probe vessels gently.
sourcesOfError: Vessels cut too short at the abattoir.
Clotted blood obscuring valves.
commonMistakes: Swapping left and right — remember the heart is labelled as if in the body facing you.
Calling the pulmonary vein an artery.
Drawing the right ventricle wall thicker.
examTips: Explain each structure's function, e.g. valves prevent backflow.
Trace blood flow in correct order through chambers and vessels — a common structured question.

checkQuestions.q: Which chamber has the thickest wall?
checkQuestions.explanation: It pumps blood to the whole body against high resistance.

checkQuestions.q: The valve between the right atrium and right ventricle is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The tricuspid valve has three flaps.

checkQuestions.q: With a stroke volume of 60 cm³ and 80 beats/min, cardiac output is
Which vessel carries oxygenated blood to the heart?
checkQuestions.explanation: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practicals.title: Effect of exercise on pulse rate
practicals.aim: To measure the pulse rate at rest and after exercise and determine the recovery time.
apparatus: Stopwatch or watch with seconds hand
safety: Students with asthma, heart or sickle-cell conditions should record data rather than exercise.
Exercise on a dry, flat surface and stop if dizzy.
procedure: Sit quietly for 5 minutes, then find the pulse at the wrist (radial artery) with two fingers, not the thumb.
Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4; repeat three times and find the mean resting rate.
Do step-ups or run on the spot for 2 minutes.
Immediately count the pulse for 15 seconds, then again every minute until it returns to the resting value.
Record results and draw a line graph of pulse rate against time.
practicals.expectedObservations: The pulse rate rises sharply after exercise and then falls gradually back to the resting rate within a few minutes. Fitter individuals return to resting rate faster.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Resting counts in 15 s: 18, 17, 19 → mean 18 → 18 × 4 = 72 beats/min.
Immediately after exercise: 32 in 15 s → 128 beats/min. Increase = (128 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100 ≈ 77.8%.
Readings at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 min: 112, 96, 84, 76, 72 beats/min → recovery time 5 minutes.
precautions: Rest before taking the resting pulse.
Use fingertips, not the thumb, which has its own pulse.
Exercise at the same intensity for all students.
sourcesOfError: Miscounting beats in short intervals.
Delay in taking the first reading after exercise.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply 15-second counts by 4.
Joining graph points with a ruler when a smooth curve is expected — follow the question.
Plotting time on the vertical axis.
examTips: Explain why: muscles need more oxygen and glucose and must remove carbon dioxide faster during exercise.
Put the independent variable (time) on the x-axis.

checkQuestions.q: A student counts 21 beats in 15 seconds. The pulse rate is
checkQuestions.explanation: 21 × 4 = 84 beats per minute.

checkQuestions.q: The pulse rises during exercise mainly to
options: supply more oxygen and glucose to muscles
checkQuestions.explanation: Active muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose.

checkQuestions.q: Why should the thumb not be used to feel the pulse?
options: It has its own pulse that can confuse the count
checkQuestions.explanation: The thumb has a noticeable pulse of its own.

practicals.title: Comparing inhaled and exhaled air
practicals.aim: To show that exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide, water vapour and heat than inhaled air, and to measure breathing rate.
apparatus: Two boiling tubes with two-holed stoppers and bent glass tubes (inhaled/exhaled air apparatus)
safety: Use a clean mouthpiece for each student.
Breathe gently and never suck lime water into the mouth.
Wash out mouthpieces with disinfectant.
procedure: Set up two tubes of lime water so that breathing in draws room air through tube A and breathing out passes through tube B.
Breathe gently in and out through the mouthpiece about 10 times.
Compare the appearance of the lime water in both tubes.
Breathe on a cool mirror and test the moisture with cobalt chloride paper.
Record room temperature, then breathe onto the thermometer bulb and record the temperature.
At rest, count breaths for one minute three times and find the mean.
practicals.expectedObservations: Lime water in the exhaled-air tube turns milky quickly; that in the inhaled-air tube stays clear or turns milky only very slowly. Mist forms on the mirror and turns cobalt chloride paper from blue to pink. Exhaled air is warmer than room air.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Typical composition: carbon dioxide 0.04% in inhaled air and about 4% in exhaled air, so exhaled air has 4 ÷ 0.04 = 100 times more carbon dioxide.
Breathing rate: 16, 15, 17 breaths per minute → mean (16 + 15 + 17) ÷ 3 = 16 breaths/min. With a tidal volume of 500 cm³, ventilation = 16 × 500 = 8000 cm³/min (8 dm³/min).
precautions: Breathe gently so lime water is not blown out or sucked in.
Use equal volumes of lime water in both tubes.
Breathe in and out the same number of times.
sourcesOfError: Unequal flow of air through the two tubes.
Moisture already on the mirror before breathing.
commonMistakes: Saying exhaled air contains no oxygen (it has about 16%).
Mixing up which tube receives exhaled air.
examTips: Name the gas and the test: carbon dioxide turns lime water milky (white precipitate of calcium carbonate).
Explain that the source of the extra carbon dioxide is tissue respiration.

checkQuestions.q: Lime water turns milky in the presence of
checkQuestions.explanation: CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate.

checkQuestions.q: Breathing counts are 18, 20 and 19 per minute. The mean is
Which statement about exhaled air is correct?
options: It is cooler than inhaled air
It contains more water vapour than inhaled air
checkQuestions.explanation: Exhaled air is warmer, moist and richer in CO₂.

practicals.title: Respiration in germinating seeds: heat and carbon dioxide
practicals.aim: To show that germinating seeds release heat and carbon dioxide during respiration.
apparatus: Conical flask with stopper and delivery tube
materials: Soaked, germinating cowpea or maize seeds
Boiled (killed) seeds rinsed in dilute disinfectant
safety: Handle hot seeds and disinfectant with care.
Do not break the glass of thermos flasks.
procedure: Soak seeds for 24 hours and allow them to start germinating.
Boil half of the seeds for 10 minutes, cool them and rinse both batches in dilute disinfectant to kill microorganisms.
Fill flask A with germinating seeds and flask B (control) with boiled seeds.
Insert a thermometer into each, plug the mouths loosely with cotton wool and invert the flasks.
Record the temperature in each flask at the start and daily for three days.
In a separate set-up, connect a flask of germinating seeds to a test tube of lime water and observe.
practicals.expectedObservations: The temperature in flask A rises steadily; the temperature in flask B stays the same as room temperature. Lime water connected to germinating seeds turns milky.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Flask A: 28.0 °C at start, 33.5 °C after 3 days. Rise = 5.5 °C; mean rise per day = 5.5 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.83 °C.
Flask B: 28.0 °C at start and 28.0 °C after 3 days → rise 0 °C.
Difference attributable to respiration = 5.5 − 0 = 5.5 °C.
precautions: Disinfect seeds so that microbial respiration does not produce heat in the control.
Invert the flasks so that heat is not lost upwards and CO₂ (denser) can escape.
Use equal quantities of seeds.
sourcesOfError: Microorganisms growing on seeds in either flask.
Thermometers not touching seeds equally.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the control flask.
Saying the heat comes from the sun.
Sealing flasks airtight so seeds run out of oxygen.
examTips: Always state the purpose of the control (to show that the change is due to living seeds).
Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.

checkQuestions.q: Why are the seeds rinsed in dilute disinfectant?
options: To kill microorganisms on their surfaces
checkQuestions.explanation: Microbes also respire and produce heat, which would affect results.

checkQuestions.q: The flask with boiled seeds is the
checkQuestions.explanation: It shows what happens without living, respiring seeds.

checkQuestions.q: Temperature rises from 27 °C to 31 °C in 2 days. The mean rise per day is
Lime water connected to germinating seeds turns milky because seeds produce
checkQuestions.explanation: CO₂ is a product of respiration.

practicals.title: Structure of the mammalian kidney
practicals.aim: To examine the external and internal (longitudinal section) structure of a goat or sheep kidney.
materials: Fresh goat, sheep or pig kidney from the abattoir
safety: Wear gloves and wash hands after handling.
Cut on a board away from the body.
Disinfect tools and benches.
procedure: Examine the outside of the kidney and note its bean shape, the hilum and any remaining blood vessels or ureter.
Measure its length and width.
Place the kidney flat and cut it lengthwise through the hilum into two equal halves.
Identify the cortex, medulla, pyramids, pelvis and ureter with a hand lens.
Draw the longitudinal section and label it.
practicals.expectedObservations: A reddish-brown, bean-shaped organ with a fibrous capsule. In section: an outer, darker granular cortex; an inner, paler striped medulla forming cone-shaped pyramids; the pyramids open into the funnel-shaped pelvis, which leads into the ureter at the hilum. The renal artery and vein enter and leave at the hilum.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Kidney length 6.5 cm, drawing 13.0 cm long → magnification = 13.0 ÷ 6.5 = ×2.
Urine formation: if the kidneys filter 180 dm³ of filtrate per day and produce 1.5 dm³ of urine, the percentage reabsorbed = (180 − 1.5) ÷ 180 × 100 ≈ 99.2%.
precautions: Cut exactly through the hilum to show all regions.
Use a sharp knife to avoid tearing.
sourcesOfError: Fat around the kidney hiding the hilum.
Section cut off-centre so the pelvis is missed.
commonMistakes: Labelling the pyramids as cortex.
Confusing the ureter with the urethra.
Omitting the magnification.
examTips: Give the function of each region: cortex (filtration in glomeruli), medulla (reabsorption, loops of Henle), pelvis (collects urine).
Spell 'ureter' and 'urethra' carefully.

checkQuestions.q: The cone-shaped regions in the medulla are the
checkQuestions.explanation: Pyramids contain collecting ducts and loops of Henle.

checkQuestions.q: Urine leaves the kidney through the
checkQuestions.explanation: The ureter carries urine to the bladder.

checkQuestions.q: Ultrafiltration takes place mainly in the
checkQuestions.explanation: Glomeruli and Bowman's capsules lie in the cortex.

practicals.title: The mammalian eye and the blind spot
practicals.aim: To examine the structure of a mammalian eye (cow or goat) and to demonstrate and measure the blind spot.
materials: Card with a cross and a dot 6 cm apart
safety: Wear gloves and wash hands afterwards.
The eye wall is tough; cut slowly and away from your fingers.
procedure: Identify the cornea, sclera, iris, pupil, optic nerve and eye muscles on the outside.
Cut around the middle (equator) of the eyeball to separate front and back halves.
Identify the lens, vitreous humour, retina, choroid and the blind spot where the optic nerve leaves.
For the blind spot test, close the left eye and stare at the cross with the right eye, holding the card at arm's length.
Slowly bring the card towards the face until the dot disappears; measure the distance from eye to card.
Repeat three times and find the mean.
practicals.expectedObservations: The lens is transparent, biconvex and firm; the retina is a thin layer that easily separates from the black choroid; there is a point where the optic nerve leaves with no light-sensitive cells. In the card test the dot disappears at about 20–30 cm and reappears when the card is moved closer.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Distances at which the dot disappeared: 25.0, 24.0 and 26.0 cm. Mean = 75.0 ÷ 3 = 25.0 cm.
The image of the dot then falls on the blind spot, where there are no rods or cones.
precautions: Keep the eye fixed on the cross throughout.
Move the card slowly.
Repeat readings and average them.
sourcesOfError: Eye moving towards the dot.
Measuring from the forehead rather than the eye.
commonMistakes: Confusing the blind spot with the yellow spot (fovea).
Saying the iris focuses light.
examTips: Link each structure to its function, e.g. ciliary muscles change lens shape (accommodation).
Explain why the dot disappears using 'no photoreceptors at the blind spot'.

checkQuestions.q: The blind spot is where
options: the optic nerve leaves the eye
checkQuestions.explanation: No rods or cones are present where the optic nerve leaves.

checkQuestions.q: Readings of 22, 24 and 23 cm give a mean of
Which structure controls the size of the pupil?
checkQuestions.explanation: The muscles of the iris change pupil diameter.

checkQuestions.q: Which part of the eye is transparent and refracts most light?
checkQuestions.explanation: The curved cornea does most of the refraction.

practicals.title: Reflex and voluntary actions: reaction time
practicals.aim: To demonstrate the knee-jerk reflex and to measure reaction time using a falling ruler.
materials: Conversion table or formula for time from distance
safety: Tap the knee gently with the side of the hand, not a hard object.
Do not let the ruler fall on toes.
procedure: Let a partner sit with one leg crossed loosely over the other and tap just below the kneecap; observe the leg.
For reaction time, the partner rests a forearm on the bench edge with thumb and finger apart at the 0 cm mark of a hanging metre rule.
Release the ruler without warning; the partner catches it as quickly as possible.
Record the distance fallen at the top of the thumb.
Repeat ten times and calculate the mean distance and reaction time.
Repeat with the partner's eyes closed while you say 'now' as you drop it.
practicals.expectedObservations: The lower leg kicks forward automatically and immediately when the tendon is tapped (reflex). In the ruler test, the catch distance becomes shorter with practice; reaction is slower when the person is distracted.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Time for a falling object: t = √(2d ÷ g), g = 9.8 m/s².
Mean catch distance 0.18 m → t = √(2 × 0.18 ÷ 9.8) = √0.03673 ≈ 0.19 s.
A distance of 0.10 m gives t = √(0.2 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.14 s.
precautions: Keep the starting position constant.
Drop without signalling (do not let the catcher anticipate).
Take many readings and average them.
sourcesOfError: Catcher anticipating the drop.
Reading the ruler at different parts of the thumb.
commonMistakes: Calling catching the ruler a reflex; it is a voluntary action involving the brain.
Forgetting to convert cm to m before using the formula.
examTips: Draw and label the reflex arc: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone (in the spinal cord), motor neurone, effector.
Distinguish reflex (spinal, automatic) from voluntary (brain, conscious) actions.

checkQuestions.q: The knee-jerk is a
checkQuestions.explanation: It is an automatic response coordinated by the spinal cord.

checkQuestions.q: A ruler falls 0.20 m before being caught. Using t = √(2d/g), with g = 10 m/s², t is
In a reflex arc, the effector in the knee-jerk is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The quadriceps muscle contracts to straighten the leg.

practicals.title: Sensitivity of the skin: two-point discrimination
practicals.aim: To compare the density of touch receptors on different parts of the skin using two-point discrimination.
apparatus: Two blunt pins or a pair of compasses/hairpin
safety: Use blunt points and press gently; do not break the skin.
Clean points with alcohol between students.
procedure: Blindfold the subject.
Touch the fingertip with the two points 10 mm apart, or randomly with one point, and ask whether one or two points are felt.
Reduce the separation in 1 mm steps and find the smallest distance at which two points are still felt.
Repeat on the palm, back of the hand, forearm and back of the neck.
Record the minimum separation for each area.
practicals.expectedObservations: Two points are distinguished at very small separations on the fingertips and lips, but only at large separations on the forearm and back of the neck.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Results: fingertip 2 mm, palm 10 mm, forearm 40 mm. The fingertip is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 times more sensitive than the forearm in this test.
Correct responses on the fingertip: 18 correct out of 20 trials = 18 ÷ 20 × 100 = 90%.
precautions: Press both points at the same time and with the same pressure.
Include random single-point touches as checks.
The subject must not see the points.
sourcesOfError: Unequal pressure of the two points.
Subject guessing.
commonMistakes: Concluding the forearm has no receptors.
Not including single-point controls.
examTips: Explain: smaller separation means touch receptors are closer together (more receptors per unit area).
Name the receptors of the skin: touch, pressure, pain, heat, cold.

checkQuestions.q: The most sensitive part to touch is usually the
checkQuestions.explanation: Fingertips have a high density of touch receptors.

checkQuestions.q: A subject is correct 12 times out of 16 trials. The percentage is
Why are random single-point touches included?
options: To check that the subject is not guessing
checkQuestions.explanation: They act as a control on the reliability of responses.

practicals.title: Structure of a flower and the floral formula
practicals.aim: To examine the parts of a complete flower (e.g. Hibiscus or Caesalpinia/pride of Barbados), draw a half-flower and write its floral formula.
materials: Fresh flowers of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, Caesalpinia pulcherrima and Crotalaria or Allamanda
safety: Cut on a tile, away from your fingers.
Wash hands after handling plant material.
procedure: Examine the whole flower and count the sepals (and epicalyx in Hibiscus), petals, stamens and carpels.
Note whether parts are free or fused, and whether the flower is radially or bilaterally symmetrical.
Cut the flower vertically through the centre into two halves.
Note the position of the ovary relative to the other floral parts (superior or inferior).
Draw the half-flower about 8–10 cm long and label it.
Write the floral formula and count the ovules in the ovary.
practicals.expectedObservations: Hibiscus: epicalyx, 5 fused sepals, 5 free large petals, many stamens fused into a staminal tube around the style, superior ovary of 5 fused carpels, 5 stigmas; radially symmetrical (actinomorphic). Caesalpinia: 5 sepals, 5 unequal petals, 10 long free stamens, one carpel; bilaterally symmetrical (zygomorphic).
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Floral formula of Hibiscus: ⊕ ⚥ Epicalyx 5–8, K(5) C5 A(∞) G(5) — brackets show fusion, a line under G shows a superior ovary.
If one Hibiscus ovary has 5 loculi with 6 ovules each, total ovules = 5 × 6 = 30, so at most 30 seeds can form.
Drawing magnification: half-flower 4.5 cm long drawn 9.0 cm → ×2.
precautions: Cut exactly through the middle of the ovary.
Use fresh flowers that are fully open.
Count parts carefully with a hand lens.
sourcesOfError: Damaged or fallen parts in older flowers.
Difficulty counting many small stamens.
commonMistakes: Drawing the whole flower when a half-flower (L.S.) is asked.
Mixing up the stigma and anther.
Omitting the epicalyx in Hibiscus.
examTips: Label: sepal, petal, stamen (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary, ovule), receptacle, pedicel.
State the function of each part, and the agent of pollination suggested by the flower's features.

checkQuestions.q: In a floral formula, K(5) means
checkQuestions.explanation: K = calyx (sepals); brackets show fusion.

checkQuestions.q: The male part of a flower is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The stamen consists of the anther and filament.

checkQuestions.q: An ovary with 4 loculi of 8 ovules each can produce at most
checkQuestions.explanation: 4 × 8 = 32 ovules, each may become a seed.

checkQuestions.q: A flower that can be cut into two equal halves along only one plane is
checkQuestions.explanation: Bilaterally symmetrical flowers are zygomorphic.

practicals.title: Insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers
practicals.aim: To compare the features of insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers and relate them to their mode of pollination.
materials: Wind-pollinated flowers: maize tassel and silk, guinea grass or elephant grass
safety: Students with pollen allergy should avoid shaking flowers near the face.
Wash hands after the practical.
procedure: Examine each flower and record colour, size, scent, nectaries, exposure of anthers and stigma, and texture of stigma.
Tap the anthers over a slide to collect pollen from each flower type.
Examine the pollen under the microscope and note its size and surface.
Measure the length of maize silk (style) and the length of the Hibiscus style.
Tabulate the differences between the two types.
practicals.expectedObservations: Insect-pollinated flowers are large, brightly coloured and scented with nectaries; anthers and stigmas are inside the flower; pollen is large, sticky and rough-walled. Wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull, unscented, without nectar; anthers hang outside on long filaments; stigmas are long and feathery; pollen is small, light, smooth and produced in large amounts.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Pollen diameter estimate at ×400 (field 400 µm): Hibiscus pollen grain fills about 1/3 of the field → about 133 µm; grass pollen fills about 1/16 → about 25 µm. Hibiscus pollen is about 133 ÷ 25 ≈ 5 times wider.
One maize tassel releases about 2 000 000 pollen grains for about 1000 ovules on a cob, i.e. about 2000 grains per ovule.
precautions: Use freshly opened flowers.
Collect pollen without contaminating one slide with another.
sourcesOfError: Estimated pollen sizes from field of view are approximate.
Old flowers lose pollen and scent.
commonMistakes: Giving 'colourful' for wind-pollinated flowers.
Listing features without linking them to pollination.
examTips: WAEC expects a table of at least four paired differences, each pair worth a mark.
Explain each feature's advantage, e.g. feathery stigma gives a large surface to trap airborne pollen.

checkQuestions.q: Which feature suggests wind pollination?

Identify the epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp, seeds and placentation.

Differences in mass between individual fruits.

practicals.title: Conditions for germination and percentage germination
practicals.aim: To show that water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are necessary for germination and to calculate percentage germination.
apparatus: Four test tubes or boiling tubes with stoppers
materials: Alkaline pyrogallol (teacher use only) or sealed boiled water
safety: Alkaline pyrogallol is corrosive; it must be handled only by the teacher.
Label all tubes clearly.
procedure: Set up tube A: seeds on moist cotton wool at room temperature (control).
Tube B: seeds on dry cotton wool (no water).
Tube C: seeds in boiled, cooled water covered with a layer of oil (no oxygen).
Tube D: seeds on moist cotton wool kept in a refrigerator (low temperature).
Use 10 seeds in each tube and leave for 4–5 days.
Count the seeds that have germinated (radicle visible) in each tube and calculate percentage germination.
practicals.expectedObservations: Seeds in tube A germinate. Seeds in B (no water), C (no oxygen) and D (cold) do not germinate or germinate very poorly.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
% germination = number germinated ÷ number sown × 100.
Tube A: 9 of 10 → 90%. Tube B: 0 of 10 → 0%. Tube C: 0 → 0%. Tube D: 1 of 10 → 10%.
A farmer's seed test: 46 of 50 seeds germinate → 46 ÷ 50 × 100 = 92% germination.
precautions: Use seeds of the same type, size and age.
Use the same number of seeds in each tube.
Keep all tubes except D at the same temperature.
sourcesOfError: Some seeds may be dead (not viable).
Air dissolving back into the boiled water.
commonMistakes: Omitting the control tube.
Saying light is necessary for germination.
Counting swollen seeds as germinated.
examTips: State the condition missing in each tube and the purpose of the oil layer (prevents oxygen from dissolving in the water).
Explain why each condition is needed: water activates enzymes, oxygen for respiration, warmth for enzyme activity.

options: prevents oxygen dissolving in the water
checkQuestions.explanation: It stops air from reaching the boiled water.

checkQuestions.explanation: It has all the conditions for germination.

practicals.aim: To observe and compare epigeal germination (e.g. cowpea, bean) and hypogeal germination (e.g. maize) and measure seedling growth.
apparatus: Boxes or pots of moist sawdust or soil
Gas jar lined with blotting paper (seed jar)
safety: Wash hands after handling soil.
procedure: Soak seeds overnight and plant some in moist sawdust; place others between blotting paper and the wall of a gas jar.
Observe every day for 7–10 days, keeping the medium moist.
Record the order in which the radicle, plumule and other parts emerge and where the cotyledons stay.
Measure the length of the plumule (shoot) each day.
Draw seedlings at 3 and 7 days, labelled.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cowpea: the hypocotyl elongates and arches, pulling the cotyledons above the soil, where they turn green (epigeal). Maize: the coleoptile pushes through the soil while the grain (cotyledon/endosperm) stays below the soil (hypogeal). The radicle always appears first.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Cowpea shoot lengths (mm) on days 2, 4, 6, 8: 5, 22, 48, 80. Growth rate between day 4 and day 8 = (80 − 22) ÷ 4 = 14.5 mm per day.
Plot length against time; the curve is S-shaped over a longer period.
precautions: Keep the medium moist but not waterlogged.
Measure from the same reference point each day.
sourcesOfError: Curved shoots are hard to measure accurately.
Seeds varying in size and vigour.
commonMistakes: Calling maize epigeal.
Confusing hypocotyl with epicotyl.
Drawing seedlings without the seed coat or remains of the grain.
examTips: Identify the elongating part in each type: hypocotyl in epigeal, epicotyl in hypogeal.
Labels: radicle, plumule, cotyledon, hypocotyl, epicotyl, coleoptile, seed coat.

checkQuestions.explanation: Elongation of the hypocotyl lifts them above the soil.

checkQuestions.explanation: The grain stays in the soil.

checkQuestions.q: A shoot grows from 12 mm to 42 mm in 5 days. The mean growth rate is
checkQuestions.explanation: (42 − 12) ÷ 5 = 6 mm per day.

practicals.title: Testing a leaf for starch: light and chlorophyll
practicals.aim: To test a leaf for starch and show that light and chlorophyll are needed for photosynthesis.
materials: Potted plant destarched for 48 hours in the dark (e.g. Coleus, Acalypha variegated)
safety: Ethanol is highly flammable: turn off the flame before placing ethanol in the hot water bath; never heat ethanol directly.
Wear eye protection.
Handle hot leaves with forceps.
procedure: Destarch the plant by keeping it in the dark for 48 hours.
Cover part of one leaf on both sides with foil; use a variegated leaf for the chlorophyll test. Expose the plant to bright light for 4–6 hours.
Detach the leaves and draw the pattern of green and white areas of the variegated leaf.
Boil each leaf in water for 1 minute to kill the cells and soften the cell walls.
Turn off the flame; place the leaf in a boiling tube of ethanol standing in the hot water until it is decolourised.
Dip the brittle leaf in warm water to soften it, spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution.
Observe and record the colours.
practicals.expectedObservations: Parts exposed to light turn blue-black (starch present); the covered part stays yellow-brown (no starch). In the variegated leaf only the formerly green parts turn blue-black; the white parts stay brown.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Area estimate on a grid: a leaf traced on 1 cm² graph paper covers 48 squares, of which 12 were covered with foil. Proportion that made starch = (48 − 12) ÷ 48 × 100 = 75%.
precautions: Destarch the plant fully before the experiment.
Turn off the flame before using ethanol.
Soften the leaf in warm water after ethanol so it does not break.
sourcesOfError: Incomplete destarching gives starch in covered areas.
Light leaking under the foil edges.
commonMistakes: Testing for glucose instead of starch.
Giving the wrong reason for boiling (it kills cells and breaks membranes so iodine can enter).
Saying ethanol removes starch — it removes chlorophyll.
examTips: Give the reason for each step; WAEC awards marks for 'why' more than 'what'.
Draw the before and after pattern of the variegated leaf to show the link with chlorophyll.

checkQuestions.q: Why is the leaf placed in hot ethanol?
checkQuestions.explanation: Ethanol dissolves chlorophyll so colour changes can be seen.

checkQuestions.q: The plant is kept in darkness for 48 hours to
checkQuestions.explanation: Destarching ensures any starch found was made during the experiment.

checkQuestions.q: Why must the flame be turned off before using ethanol?
checkQuestions.explanation: Ethanol vapour ignites easily.

checkQuestions.q: The white part of a variegated leaf stays brown with iodine because it lacks
checkQuestions.explanation: No chlorophyll means no photosynthesis and no starch.

practicals.title: Effect of light intensity on oxygen production by a water plant
practicals.aim: To investigate how the distance of a lamp (light intensity) affects the rate of photosynthesis of a water plant measured by counting bubbles.
materials: Pond water or water with a little sodium hydrogencarbonate
safety: Keep the lamp and electrical leads away from water.
Handle the glowing splint carefully.
procedure: Place the cut water plant under an inverted funnel in a beaker of water with a pinch of sodium hydrogencarbonate.
Place a test tube full of water over the funnel stem to collect gas.
Put the lamp 10 cm from the beaker and allow 5 minutes to adjust.
Count the bubbles released per minute three times and find the mean.
Repeat at 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm, keeping temperature constant.
Test the collected gas with a glowing splint.
practicals.expectedObservations: The number of bubbles per minute falls as the lamp is moved further away. The collected gas relights a glowing splint, showing it is mainly oxygen.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Light intensity is proportional to 1/d². Results: 10 cm → 40 bubbles/min; 20 cm → 18; 30 cm → 9; 40 cm → 5; 50 cm → 3.
Relative intensity at 20 cm compared with 10 cm = (10 ÷ 20)² = 0.25. Rate fell from 40 to 18, i.e. by (40 − 18) ÷ 40 × 100 = 55%.
precautions: Keep the temperature constant (place a water trough or heat filter between lamp and beaker).
Allow time for adjustment at each distance.
Use the same piece of plant throughout.
sourcesOfError: Bubbles differ in size.
Background light in the room.
Heat from the lamp increasing the rate.
commonMistakes: Saying the gas is carbon dioxide.
Not stating that temperature was controlled.
Plotting distance when the question asks for light intensity.
examTips: Identify the dependent (bubbles/min), independent (distance or light intensity) and controlled variables.
Explain the purpose of sodium hydrogencarbonate (supplies carbon dioxide).

checkQuestions.q: The gas that relights a glowing splint is
checkQuestions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion.

checkQuestions.q: Moving the lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm reduces light intensity to
checkQuestions.explanation: Intensity ∝ 1/d², so (10/20)² = 1/4.

checkQuestions.explanation: It releases CO₂ for photosynthesis.

practicals.title: Food tests: starch, reducing sugar, protein, fat
practicals.aim: To carry out standard tests for starch, reducing sugars, non-reducing sugars, proteins and fats (oils) on food samples.
materials: Samples: yam or garri slurry, glucose, sugar (sucrose), egg white, groundnut oil, unknown solutions
safety: Wear eye protection when heating and when using sodium hydroxide.
Point test tubes away from people while heating.
Ethanol and Sudan III are flammable; keep away from flames.
procedure: Starch: add 2–3 drops of iodine to 2 cm³ of the sample.
Reducing sugar: add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to 2 cm³ of sample and heat in a boiling water bath for 5 minutes.

Non-reducing sugar: if the Benedict's test is negative, boil a fresh sample with 1 cm³ dilute hydrochloric acid for 2 minutes, cool, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, then repeat the Benedict's test.
Protein (Biuret): add 1 cm³ sodium hydroxide to 2 cm³ of sample, then 2 drops of 1% copper(II) sulphate, and shake.
Fat: rub the sample on filter paper and hold it up to the light; or add Sudan III, or shake with ethanol then pour into water (emulsion test).
Record the test, observation and inference for each sample in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Starch: blue-black. Reducing sugar: blue solution turns green, yellow, orange then brick-red precipitate. Non-reducing sugar: brick-red only after acid hydrolysis. Protein: violet/purple colour. Fat: translucent spot on paper; red-stained oil layer with Sudan III; milky-white emulsion in the ethanol test.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Semi-quantitative reducing sugar: precipitate colours rank concentration: green < yellow < orange < brick-red.
Dilution: to make 10 cm³ of a 0.5% glucose solution from a 2% stock, volume of stock = 0.5 × 10 ÷ 2 = 2.5 cm³, made up with 7.5 cm³ water.
precautions: Use clean test tubes for each test.
Heat Benedict's tests in a water bath, not directly.
Use only a little copper(II) sulphate in the Biuret test so the blue does not mask the violet.
Neutralise the acid before the Benedict's test for non-reducing sugar.
sourcesOfError: Contaminated test tubes.
Insufficient heating time.
Colour judgment varies between students.
commonMistakes: Writing 'red colour' instead of 'brick-red precipitate'.
Testing sucrose directly with Benedict's and calling it a reducing sugar.
Mixing up the table columns test / observation / inference.
examTips: Use the three-column table: Test, Observation, Inference — inferences must follow from observations.
State the reagent, the procedure and the result for full marks.

checkQuestions.q: A brick-red precipitate after heating with Benedict's solution indicates
checkQuestions.explanation: Reducing sugars reduce copper(II) to red copper(I) oxide.

checkQuestions.q: The Biuret test for protein gives a
checkQuestions.explanation: Peptide bonds react with copper ions in alkali to form a violet complex.

checkQuestions.q: Sucrose gives a brick-red precipitate only after
options: boiling with dilute acid and neutralising
checkQuestions.explanation: Acid hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose, which are reducing sugars.

practicals.title: Action of salivary amylase on starch and the effect of temperature
practicals.aim: To show that salivary amylase digests starch to reducing sugar and to investigate the effect of temperature on its activity.
apparatus: Water baths at about 10 °C (ice), 37 °C and boiling
materials: Saliva solution (rinse mouth with water and collect into a clean beaker; dilute)
safety: Each student uses only their own saliva and washes apparatus with disinfectant after use.
Take care with boiling water baths.
procedure: Put drops of iodine solution in the wells of a spotting tile.
Place 5 cm³ starch solution and 1 cm³ saliva in separate tubes in each water bath for 5 minutes to reach temperature.
Mix the saliva with the starch in each bath and start the stopwatch.
Every 30 seconds remove a drop of each mixture and add it to a fresh iodine well.
Record the time when the iodine no longer turns blue-black (end point).
Set up a control with boiled saliva; at the end, test the 37 °C mixture with Benedict's solution.
practicals.expectedObservations: At 37 °C the blue-black colour disappears quickly (iodine stays brown) and the mixture gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's. At 10 °C the change is slow. With boiled saliva, the blue-black colour persists: the enzyme has been denatured.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Time to end point: 10 °C → 600 s; 37 °C → 90 s; 80 °C (boiled) → no end point.
Rate = 1000 ÷ time: 10 °C → 1000 ÷ 600 ≈ 1.7 s⁻¹ (arbitrary units); 37 °C → 1000 ÷ 90 ≈ 11.1. The enzyme works about 600 ÷ 90 ≈ 6.7 times faster at 37 °C than at 10 °C.
precautions: Equilibrate solutions to temperature before mixing.
Use a clean dropper each time.
Use the same volumes and concentrations in all tubes.
sourcesOfError: Temperature of water baths changing.
Judging the end-point colour.
commonMistakes: Saying the enzyme is 'killed' — enzymes are denatured, not killed.
Not including a control.
Saying low temperature denatures the enzyme (it only slows it).
examTips: Name the substrate (starch), enzyme (amylase/ptyalin) and product (maltose).
Explain the optimum temperature with kinetic energy and denaturation of the active site.

checkQuestions.q: Salivary amylase converts starch into
checkQuestions.explanation: Amylase hydrolyses starch to the disaccharide maltose.

checkQuestions.q: In the boiled-saliva tube, iodine stays blue-black because
checkQuestions.explanation: High temperature destroys the shape of the active site.

practicals.title: Mammalian skulls, teeth and dental formulae
practicals.aim: To examine the skulls and teeth of a herbivore and a carnivore, write their dental formulae and relate tooth structure to diet.
materials: Cleaned skulls of a goat or sheep (herbivore) and a dog (carnivore)
Human tooth models or extracted teeth (from a dental clinic, sterilised)
safety: Use only cleaned and disinfected specimens.
Wash hands after handling.
procedure: Examine the jaws of each skull and identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars.
Count each type of tooth in one half of the upper and lower jaws.
Write the dental formula and calculate the total number of teeth.
Note special features: diastema, horny pad, carnassial teeth, ridged molars.
Draw the side view of the lower jaw of each skull.
practicals.expectedObservations: Goat/sheep: no upper incisors or canines (a horny pad instead), lower canines look like incisors, a gap (diastema) between front teeth and cheek teeth, broad ridged premolars and molars for grinding. practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Goat: i 0/3, c 0/1, pm 3/3, m 3/3. Teeth per half = upper 0+0+3+3 = 6, lower 3+1+3+3 = 10 → 16; total = 16 × 2 = 32.
Dog: i 3/3, c 1/1, pm 4/4, m 2/3. Half = upper 10, lower 11 → 21; total = 42.
Human adult: i 2/2, c 1/1, pm 2/2, m 3/3 → 16 per half → 32.

Distinguish missing (fallen) teeth from teeth that are naturally absent by looking for sockets.

Young animals having milk teeth or unerupted molars.

Writing the whole-jaw count on the formula.
Calling the goat's lower canines incisors without comment.

Relate each feature to diet, e.g. the diastema allows the tongue to move food.

practicals.title: Dissection of a rat to display the alimentary system
practicals.aim: To dissect a freshly killed rat (or examine a preserved specimen) to display the alimentary canal and associated organs.

Lift the skin at the lower abdomen with forceps and cut along the midline up to the jaw, then cut sideways at each end.
Pin back the skin, then cut the muscle wall in the same way to expose the abdominal organs.

Preserved specimens are discoloured and stiff.

Labelling a gall bladder in a rat.
Using unruled label lines that cross.

State the function of each labelled organ if asked.

practicals.title: Measuring ecological factors in a habitat
practicals.aim: To use simple instruments to measure abiotic factors (temperature, rainfall, humidity, light, wind, soil pH) in two habitats in the school compound.

Read air temperature at 1 m above the ground and soil temperature at 10 cm depth at each site at the same time of day.
Read the wet- and dry-bulb thermometers and use the table to find relative humidity.
