practicals.title: Quadrat sampling of plant populations
practicals.aim: To estimate the density, frequency and percentage cover of plant species on a grassland or school field using quadrats.
materials: Identification guide to local weeds and grasses
safety: Look out for snakes, scorpions and biting ants; wear covered shoes.
Avoid throwing quadrats towards people.
procedure: Mark out the study area (e.g. 20 m × 20 m) with pegs and tapes along two edges.
Use random numbers as coordinates to place 10 quadrats.
In each quadrat count the individuals of each species (e.g. Tridax, Sida, Euphorbia hirta).
Record whether each species is present (for frequency) and estimate its percentage cover.
Calculate density, frequency and estimated total population for each species.
practicals.expectedObservations: Some species, such as grasses, occur in nearly all quadrats with high cover; others occur in few quadrats. Counts vary from quadrat to quadrat.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Tridax counts in 10 quadrats: 4, 0, 6, 3, 5, 2, 0, 7, 4, 9 → total 40.
Density = 40 ÷ 10 m² = 4 plants per m².
Frequency = present in 8 of 10 quadrats = 80%.
Estimated population in 400 m² = 4 × 400 = 1600 plants.
precautions: Place quadrats randomly to avoid bias.

Identify species carefully.

Difficulty counting grasses as individuals.

Forgetting the unit per m².
Choosing quadrat positions by eye.

practicals.title: Capture–recapture estimate of an animal population
practicals.aim: To estimate the population of a mobile animal (e.g. snails, grasshoppers, or a bean model) using the capture–mark–release–recapture (Lincoln index) method.
materials: Garden snails (Achatina) or grasshoppers; or a bag of beans as a classroom model
safety: Handle animals gently and release them where caught.
Wash hands after handling snails (risk of parasites).
procedure: Search a defined area for a fixed time and capture as many animals as possible.
Count them (first sample, n₁) and mark each with a small dot of paint where it will not affect survival.
Release them in the same area and allow 24 hours for mixing.
Capture a second sample in the same way and time (n₂).
Count the marked animals in the second sample (m).
Estimate the population N = n₁ × n₂ ÷ m.
practicals.expectedObservations: Only a proportion of the second sample carries marks. The more marked animals recaptured, the smaller the estimated population.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
First capture n₁ = 40 snails marked and released. Second capture n₂ = 36, of which m = 12 are marked.
N = 40 × 36 ÷ 12 = 1440 ÷ 12 = 120 snails.
precautions: Use marks that are not toxic and do not make animals more visible to predators.
Allow time for marked animals to mix.
Sample with the same effort each time.
sourcesOfError: Births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples.
Marks rubbing off.
Marked animals being easier or harder to catch.
commonMistakes: Using N = n₁ × m ÷ n₂.
Applying the method to plants, which do not move.
Ignoring the assumptions.
examTips: List the assumptions: no migration, births or deaths; marks not lost; marked animals mix evenly.
Show the formula before substituting.

checkQuestions.q: 50 animals are marked; a second catch of 40 contains 10 marked. The population estimate is
Which is an assumption of the method?
options: No immigration or emigration between samples
checkQuestions.explanation: The population must stay closed between samples.

checkQuestions.q: The capture–recapture method is suitable for
checkQuestions.explanation: Quadrats are used for plants; capture–recapture for mobile animals.

practicals.title: Adaptive features of plants and animals to their habitats
practicals.aim: To examine specimens of xerophytes, hydrophytes and animals and identify features that adapt them to their habitats.
materials: Water lettuce (Pistia), water lily (Nymphaea) or Salvinia (hydrophytes)
safety: Cactus spines and Euphorbia latex can injure skin and eyes; use gloves and forceps.
Wash hands after handling animals.
procedure: Examine each plant and record features related to water loss or water life: spines, thick cuticle, succulent stem, sunken stomata, air spaces, floating leaves, long petioles.
Cut a transverse section of a water lily petiole and observe air spaces.
Examine each animal and record features adapting it to water, land or both.
Tabulate specimen, habitat, adaptive feature and its function.
Draw the cactus and the water lettuce and label adaptive features.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cactus: leaves reduced to spines, green swollen stem storing water, thick waxy cuticle. Water lettuce: rosette of spongy floating leaves with hairs that repel water. Water lily: large flat leaves with stomata on the upper surface, long flexible petioles with large air spaces. Tilapia: streamlined body, fins, gills, scales. Toad: webbed hind feet, moist skin. Agama: dry scaly skin to reduce water loss.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Surface area to volume: a cactus stem approximated as a cylinder of radius 5 cm and height 20 cm has volume πr²h = 3.142 × 25 × 20 ≈ 1571 cm³ and side area 2πrh = 2 × 3.142 × 5 × 20 ≈ 628 cm²; ratio ≈ 0.40 cm⁻¹ — a low ratio reduces water loss.
Air space estimate: 45 of 100 grid squares over a water lily petiole section are air spaces → 45%.
precautions: Use fresh specimens so features are visible.
Handle spiny plants with gloves.
sourcesOfError: Damaged specimens lose hairs or cuticle.
Estimates of air spaces by eye are approximate.
commonMistakes: Listing features without functions.
Saying hydrophytes have stomata on the lower surface of floating leaves.
examTips: Use the format: feature — how it adapts the organism — e.g. 'leaves reduced to spines — reduce surface area for transpiration'.
Give observable features of the specimen in front of you.

checkQuestions.q: In cactus, leaves reduced to spines help to
checkQuestions.explanation: Small surface area reduces transpiration; spines also deter animals.

checkQuestions.q: The large air spaces in water lily petioles
options: provide buoyancy and allow gas exchange
checkQuestions.explanation: Aerenchyma helps leaves float and lets gases diffuse.

checkQuestions.q: Stomata on a floating water lily leaf are mainly found on the
checkQuestions.explanation: The lower surface is in contact with water.

practicals.title: Food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids from field data
practicals.aim: To construct food chains and webs from observed feeding relationships and draw pyramids of numbers and energy to scale.
apparatus: Sweep net and pooters (for collecting data)
materials: Field notes or data of organisms in a grassland or pond
safety: Wear covered shoes and gloves when collecting; avoid stinging insects.
procedure: Record the organisms found in a habitat and what each feeds on (observed or from reliable references).
Write at least three food chains with arrows pointing from food to feeder.
Combine the chains into a food web.
Assign each organism to a trophic level.
Use the count or energy data provided to draw pyramids of numbers and energy to scale on graph paper.
practicals.expectedObservations: Grassland: grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk; grass → caterpillar → bird; grass → goat → man. Numbers and energy decrease at each higher trophic level. A pyramid of numbers can be inverted (e.g. one mango tree supporting many insects) but a pyramid of energy is always upright.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Energy at each level (kJ/m²/year): producers 20 000; primary consumers 2 000; secondary 200; tertiary 20.
Efficiency of transfer from producers to primary consumers = 2000 ÷ 20 000 × 100 = 10%.
Scale: 1 mm bar width = 100 kJ gives bars of 200 mm, 20 mm, 2 mm and 0.2 mm; so a log scale or different scale is needed to show the top level.
precautions: Arrows must show the direction of energy flow (from eaten to eater).
Use a stated scale for pyramids.
sourcesOfError: Incomplete sampling misses organisms.
Feeding relationships assumed rather than observed.
commonMistakes: Drawing arrows from predator to prey.
Starting food chains with the sun or with an animal.
Calling decomposers a trophic level of the chain without explanation.
examTips: Name the producer, primary, secondary and tertiary consumers for a given chain.
Explain why energy is lost (respiration, heat, excretion, uneaten parts).

checkQuestions.q: In grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, the secondary consumer is the
checkQuestions.explanation: The lizard eats the primary consumer (grasshopper).

checkQuestions.q: If producers fix 15 000 kJ and primary consumers obtain 1500 kJ, the efficiency is
Which pyramid is never inverted?
checkQuestions.explanation: Energy always decreases along a chain.

checkQuestions.q: Arrows in a food chain point
options: from the eaten to the eater
checkQuestions.explanation: They show the direction of energy flow.

practicals.title: Growing microorganisms: bread mould and bacteria from the air
practicals.aim: To grow bread mould (Rhizopus) and bacterial colonies from air and fingers on nutrient agar and observe the effect of hygiene.
apparatus: Sterile Petri dishes with nutrient agar
safety: Never open sealed plates after incubation; cultures may contain pathogens.
Incubate at no more than 30 °C to avoid growing human pathogens.
Tape lids with two short strips (not completely sealed) and dispose of plates by autoclaving or soaking in strong disinfectant.
procedure: Moisten a slice of bread, expose it to air for 30 minutes, then keep it in a polythene bag in a warm dark place for 3–5 days.
Label four agar plates on the base: control, air, unwashed finger and washed finger.
Leave the 'air' plate open for 20 minutes; touch the others lightly with a finger before and after washing with soap; leave the control unopened.
Tape the lids, invert the plates and incubate at 25–30 °C for 2–3 days.
Count the colonies on each plate without opening them and describe their colour and shape.
Examine the bread mould with a hand lens and a little under the microscope (teacher-prepared slide).
practicals.expectedObservations: Bread develops white cottony threads (hyphae) with black pin-head sporangia. The air and unwashed-finger plates show many round colonies of bacteria (shiny, creamy) and some fungi (fluffy); the washed-finger plate has fewer colonies; the control has none.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Colonies: unwashed finger 64, washed finger 12. Percentage reduction = (64 − 12) ÷ 64 × 100 = 81.25%.
Bacterial growth: one bacterium dividing every 20 minutes gives 2^9 = 512 cells after 3 hours (9 generations).
precautions: Use aseptic technique: flame the loop, open lids only slightly and briefly.
Label plates on the base, not the lid.
Incubate plates upside down so condensation does not drip on colonies.
sourcesOfError: Contamination from poor aseptic technique.
Unequal pressure of finger contact.
commonMistakes: Opening plates after incubation to smell or touch them.
Leaving out the control plate.
Calling Rhizopus a bacterium.
examTips: Explain the purpose of each aseptic step.
Relate results to personal hygiene and food preservation.

checkQuestions.q: Why are agar plates incubated upside down?
options: To stop condensation dripping onto the colonies
checkQuestions.explanation: Water droplets from the lid would spread colonies.

checkQuestions.explanation: Sporangia of Rhizopus contain spores.

checkQuestions.explanation: Pathogens grow best near 37 °C.

Read the scale at eye level.

Rounding errors.

Using a bar chart for discontinuous data and calling it a histogram.
Unequal class intervals.

Label axes with units and give the graph a title.

practicals.title: Discontinuous variation: tongue rolling and blood groups
practicals.aim: To survey discontinuous characters in a class, such as tongue rolling and ABO blood groups (from records), and present the results.
materials: Blood group records from school health cards (with consent) — no blood sampling in class
safety: Do not take blood samples in the class practical; use existing records with permission.
Respect privacy; record data anonymously.
procedure: Ask each student to try to roll the tongue into a U-shape; record roller or non-roller.
Record each student's blood group from health records (anonymously).
Tally the results and calculate percentages.
Draw a bar chart (with gaps) for blood groups.
Draw a pie chart for tongue rolling.

Class of 40: rollers 26, non-rollers 14. Rollers = 26 ÷ 40 × 100 = 65%. Pie chart angle = 26 ÷ 40 × 360 = 234°; non-rollers = 126°.

Errors in health records.

practicals.title: Probability in genetics: a model monohybrid cross
practicals.aim: To use beads (or coins) to model gamete formation and fertilisation in a monohybrid cross and compare observed ratios with the expected 3 : 1 ratio.
materials: 100 red beads (dominant allele T) and 100 white beads (recessive allele t), all the same size
Or two coins (head = T, tail = t)
safety: Keep beads off the floor to avoid slipping.
procedure: Put 50 red and 50 white beads in each beaker to represent gametes from two heterozygous (Tt) parents.
Without looking, pick one bead from each beaker and record the pair (TT, Tt or tt).
Return the beads to their beakers and shake.
Repeat 100 times.
Count genotypes and phenotypes and calculate the ratios.
Combine class results and compare with the expected ratio.
practicals.expectedObservations: The three genotypes appear in approximately 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypes approximately 3 tall : 1 short. Larger samples (class totals) are closer to the expected ratio.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Results from 100 draws: TT 23, Tt 52, tt 25. Phenotypes: tall (TT + Tt) = 75, short = 25 → ratio 75 : 25 = 3 : 1.
Probability of tt from Tt × Tt = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 0.25. Expected tt in 100 = 25.
Test cross Tt × tt gives 1/2 Tt : 1/2 tt, i.e. 1 tall : 1 short.
precautions: Draw without looking.
Return beads after each draw to keep probabilities constant.
Use many trials.
sourcesOfError: Chance deviation in small samples.
Beads not mixed thoroughly.
commonMistakes: Writing the ratio of genotypes as 3 : 1.
Not returning beads, which changes the probabilities.
Writing gametes with two alleles.
examTips: Set out crosses fully: parental phenotypes, genotypes, gametes (circled), Punnett square, F1 genotypes and phenotypes, ratio.
Use a capital letter for dominant and the same small letter for recessive alleles.

checkQuestions.explanation: Three-quarters show the dominant trait.

practicals.title: Life cycles of insects: complete and incomplete metamorphosis
practicals.aim: To identify the stages in the life cycles of the housefly (complete metamorphosis) and the grasshopper or cockroach (incomplete metamorphosis).
materials: Preserved housefly eggs, larvae (maggots), pupae and adults
Grasshopper or cockroach nymphs and adults
safety: Handle preserved specimens with forceps; formalin/alcohol irritates skin.
Wash hands after handling flies and maggots.
procedure: Examine each stage with a hand lens and record size, colour, presence of legs, wings and mouthparts.
Arrange the stages of each insect in order.
Measure the length of each stage.
Draw the larva, pupa and adult housefly and a nymph and adult grasshopper.
Compare the two types of metamorphosis in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Housefly: tiny white banana-shaped eggs; cream, legless, segmented maggots, pointed at the head end; brown, barrel-shaped, immobile pupae (puparia); adults with one pair of wings, sponging mouthparts and large compound eyes. Lengths: maggot 10 mm, pupa 6 mm, adult 7 mm. The pupa is 6 ÷ 10 × 100 = 60% of the maggot's length.
Life cycle timing at 30 °C: egg 1 day, larva 5 days, pupa 4 days → egg to adult ≈ 10 days, so about 3 generations per month.
precautions: Keep specimens moist with preservative while examining.
Measure along the body axis.
sourcesOfError: Shrinkage of preserved specimens.
Damaged legs or wings.
commonMistakes: Calling a maggot a worm.
Giving the housefly two pairs of wings.
Including a pupal stage for grasshoppers.
examTips: Link each housefly stage to control: covering refuse, insecticides, destroying breeding sites.
State observable differences between larva and nymph.

checkQuestions.q: Which insect shows incomplete metamorphosis?
checkQuestions.explanation: Grasshoppers go egg → nymph → adult.

checkQuestions.q: Housefly larvae are best controlled by
checkQuestions.explanation: Maggots breed in refuse and decaying matter.

practicals.title: Specimens showing biological associations
practicals.aim: To examine specimens showing parasitism, symbiosis (mutualism), commensalism and saprophytism and state the benefit or harm to each partner.
materials: Cowpea or groundnut root with nodules
Lichen on a tree bark or wall
Epiphytic fern or orchid on a tree
safety: Handle preserved parasites with forceps and gloves.
Wash hands after handling soil and specimens.
procedure: Examine each specimen and identify the organisms involved.
Cut a root nodule open and note its pink/red interior.
Note the attachment structures: haustoria of mistletoe and dodder, hooks and suckers of tapeworm, mouthparts of ticks.
Classify each association and state how each partner is affected.
Draw the root nodules on a cowpea root and the scolex of a tapeworm.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cowpea roots bear rounded nodules with pink interiors containing Rhizobium bacteria (mutualism). Lichen: a crusty grey-green growth of an alga and fungus (mutualism). Mistletoe: green leaves (photosynthesises) but haustoria penetrate the host xylem (partial parasite). Dodder: yellow, leafless, twining stem with haustoria (total parasite). practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Nodule count: five cowpea plants have 24, 31, 18, 27 and 30 nodules → mean = 130 ÷ 5 = 26 nodules per plant.
If a nodulated legume crop fixes 100 kg N per hectare per season, a 0.25 ha plot gains 100 × 0.25 = 25 kg of nitrogen.
precautions: Dig legume roots out gently so that nodules are not lost.
Use fresh specimens.
sourcesOfError: Nodules broken off when uprooting.
Confusing nodules with gall-causing nematode swellings.
commonMistakes: Calling mistletoe a total parasite.
Calling lichen a single organism.
Not stating the benefit to both partners in mutualism.
examTips: Use a table: association, organisms, type, benefit/harm to each.
Give the adaptive features of parasites: hooks, suckers, thick cuticle, many eggs, haustoria.

checkQuestions.explanation: Bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant and receive sugars and shelter.

practicals.title: Soil: water retention, air content and humus
practicals.aim: To compare sandy, loamy and clay soils for water retention, air content and organic matter (humus) content.
apparatus: Bunsen burner, tripod and pipe-clay triangle
materials: Dry sandy, loamy and clay soils
safety: Use tongs for hot crucibles.
Heat in a ventilated room.
procedure: Water retention: put 100 g of each dry soil into funnels plugged with cotton wool; pour 100 cm³ of water onto each and collect the drainage for 30 minutes.
Record the volume collected and calculate water retained.
Air content: add 50 cm³ of dry soil to 50 cm³ of water in a measuring cylinder, stir to release air and read the final volume.
Humus: weigh an oven-dried soil sample in a crucible, heat strongly for 20 minutes, cool and reweigh; repeat to constant mass.
Calculate percentage water retained, air content and organic matter for each soil.
practicals.expectedObservations: Water drains fastest through sandy soil and most is collected; clay retains most water. Bubbles escape when soils are added to water. Loamy soil loses the most mass on heating as its humus burns off.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Water collected after 30 min: sand 70 cm³, loam 52 cm³, clay 38 cm³ → retained = 30, 48, 62 cm³ (or g).
Air content of loam: 50 cm³ soil + 50 cm³ water → 86 cm³. Air = 100 − 86 = 14 cm³; % air = 14 ÷ 50 × 100 = 28%.
Humus: crucible 20.00 g; crucible + dry soil 30.00 g; after heating 29.40 g. Loss = 0.60 g in 10.00 g soil → 6.0% organic matter.
precautions: Use the same mass of dry soil and volume of water for each sample.
Use oven-dried soil for the humus test.
Heat to constant mass.
sourcesOfError: Water held by cotton wool.
Some air trapped in clay lumps.
Loss of mineral water of crystallisation on strong heating.
commonMistakes: Confusing water drained with water retained.
Using wet soil for the humus test.
Calculating air % on the total cylinder volume instead of the soil volume.

checkQuestions.explanation: Fine clay particles have tiny pores that hold water strongly.

Wash hands afterwards.

practicals.title: Tropic responses: phototropism and geotropism
practicals.topic: Irritability as a Basic Characteristic of Protoplasm
practicals.aim: To demonstrate that shoots grow towards light and that roots grow downwards in response to gravity, using a clinostat as control.
apparatus: Light-proof box with a slit on one side
safety: Keep electrical clinostats away from water.
Handle pins carefully.
procedure: Phototropism: place a pot of seedlings in the box lit from one side; keep a control pot in uniform light or on a rotating clinostat.
Geotropism: pin soaked bean seedlings with radicles pointing in different directions to a cork kept moist in a gas jar.
Fix a similar set on a clinostat rotating horizontally (control).
Leave for 3–5 days.
Record the direction of growth and measure the angle of curvature of shoots and roots.
Draw the results.
practicals.expectedObservations: Shoots in one-sided light bend towards the light (positive phototropism); control shoots grow straight. Radicles on the stationary cork curve downwards whatever their starting direction (positive geotropism); those on the rotating clinostat grow straight in the direction they were placed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Angle of curvature measured with a protractor: day 1: 10°, day 2: 25°, day 3: 40° → mean rate = 40 ÷ 3 ≈ 13.3° per day.
Number of radicles curving down: 9 of 10 → 90%.
precautions: Keep seedlings moist.
Ensure the box is light-proof except for the slit.
Use a control in each experiment.

practicals.title: Organs of vegetative reproduction and perennation
practicals.aim: To examine storage and vegetative propagation organs and identify their nature (root, stem or leaf) and the features used for reproduction.
safety: Cut on a tile, away from fingers.
Some cocoyam varieties cause itching; wear gloves.
procedure: Examine each organ externally for buds (eyes), nodes, scale leaves, adventitious roots and scars.
Cut each across and add iodine to test for stored starch.
Decide whether each is a modified stem, root or leaf, giving evidence.
Plant pieces with buds in moist soil and observe sprouting over two weeks.
Draw an onion bulb in longitudinal section and a ginger rhizome.
practicals.expectedObservations: Irish potato has eyes (buds) in the axils of scale leaf scars — a stem tuber. Cassava and sweet potato have no nodes or buds on the tuber body — root tubers. Onion bulb has fleshy leaf bases on a short stem. Ginger rhizome is horizontal with nodes, scale leaves and buds. Cocoyam corm is vertical with rings of scale leaves. Most cut surfaces turn blue-black with iodine. Bryophyllum leaves form plantlets along the margins.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Sprouting test: 20 Irish potato pieces with an eye each; 17 sprouted → 85%. Seed yam: a 1.2 kg yam cut into 200 g setts gives 1200 ÷ 200 = 6 setts.
precautions: Make sure each planted piece has at least one bud.
Keep soil moist but not waterlogged.
sourcesOfError: Rotting of cut pieces.
Dormant buds not sprouting within the observation period.
commonMistakes: Calling cassava a stem tuber.
Confusing a corm with a bulb.
Not giving evidence for the classification.
examTips: Give the evidence: nodes, internodes, buds and scale leaves show a stem; their absence shows a root.
List advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
